## Proof

Let $X, Y, Z$ be i.i.d. standard normal random variables. We compute $P(X > YZ)$.

**Key symmetry.** Consider the transformation
$$T:(X,Y,Z)\mapsto (-X,-Y,Z).$$
Since $X,Y,Z$ are independent standard normals, the joint distribution of $(X,Y,Z)$ is invariant under $T$ (each component remains an independent standard normal: $-X,-Y,Z$ are again i.i.d. $N(0,1)$).

Now examine what $T$ does to the event $\{X > YZ\}$:
$$X > YZ \;\Longleftrightarrow\; -X < -YZ \;\Longleftrightarrow\; -X < (-Y)Z.$$
So $T$ maps the event $\{X > YZ\}$ bijectively onto $\{-X < (-Y)Z\}$, i.e. onto $\{X' < Y'Z'\}$ where $(X',Y',Z')=T(X,Y,Z)$. By distributional invariance,
$$P(X > YZ) \;=\; P(X' < Y'Z') \;=\; P(X < YZ).$$

**The boundary has probability zero.** The random variable $X - YZ$ is continuous (it is a function of the continuous random vector $(X,Y,Z)$ with a density), so
$$P(X = YZ) = P(X - YZ = 0) = 0.$$

**Conclusion.** The two events $\{X>YZ\}$ and $\{X<YZ\}$ partition the whole space up to a null set, and they have equal probability:
$$P(X>YZ) + P(X<YZ) + P(X=YZ) = 1,\qquad P(X>YZ)=P(X<YZ),\qquad P(X=YZ)=0.$$
Hence
$$2\,P(X>YZ)=1,\qquad P(X>YZ)=\tfrac{1}{2}.$$

$$\boxed{P(X > YZ) = \dfrac{1}{2}}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
